questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between implicit animations and explicit animations in SwiftUI?

options.text: Implicit animations scope to a specific view, while explicit animations wrap state mutations.
options.explanation: Implicit animations use .animation(_:value:) on a view, while explicit animations wrap state with withAnimation.

options.text: Implicit animations run on background threads, while explicit animations run on GPU hardware.
options.explanation: Both animation styles calculate layout on the main thread and render on GPU compositor layers.

options.text: Implicit animations require UIKit bridging, while explicit animations are native SwiftUI.
options.explanation: Both implicit and explicit animations are completely native SwiftUI features.

options.text: Implicit animations only execute on iPad devices in split screen mode.
options.explanation: Both animation styles operate consistently across all Apple platforms and form factors.

options.text: It lacked scoping and triggered accidentally on any parent view invalidation.
options.explanation: Without a value parameter, the modifier responded to every ancestor redraw, causing glitchy animations.

options.text: It crashed the application when used inside a NavigationView container.
options.explanation: The modifier compiled and functioned, but produced frequent unintended visual side-effects.

options.text: It disabled all gesture recognizers attached to child views.
options.explanation: Gesture handling was unaffected by the older animation modifier.

questions.prompt: What is required for a .transition() modifier to animate when a view appears or disappears?

options.text: The parent view must conform to the EquatableView protocol.
options.explanation: EquatableView conformance is not required for view transitions.

options.text: The state change causing insertion or removal must occur within an animated context.
options.explanation: Transitions only animate if the boolean state toggle is performed within withAnimation.

options.text: The transition duration must be configured to at least three seconds.
options.explanation: Transitions can run with any valid animation duration or spring preset.

questions.prompt: How does modifier order influence the behavior of the .animation(_:value:) modifier?

options.text: Modifier order has no effect on which view properties are animated.
options.explanation: In SwiftUI, modifier ordering strictly dictates which properties receive animation.

options.text: Only modifiers placed after the .animation call are interpolated across frames.
options.explanation: Modifiers placed after the animation call do not receive animation.

options.text: Placing modifiers after .animation causes a fatal compile-time syntax error.
options.explanation: Modifiers placed after .animation compile cleanly but update immediately without animating.

options.text: Only modifiers placed before .animation in the chain are animated when the value changes.

questions.prompt: Why are spring animations preferred over linear easing curves in modern iOS applications?

options.text: Springs preserve momentum when interrupted, preventing jarring visual stops.
options.explanation: Physical spring models maintain existing velocity when redirected by gestures or state updates.

options.text: Springs consume fewer CPU clock cycles than linear mathematical formulas.
options.explanation: Animation curves have negligible CPU differences on modern processors.

options.text: Springs automatically prevent views from updating their internal state.
options.explanation: Spring animations govern visual interpolation, not state mutation logic.

options.text: Linear animations were formally banned in iOS 16 App Store guidelines.
options.explanation: Linear animations remain available and supported across SwiftUI APIs.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a property animation and a view transition?

options.text: Property animations interpolate values on existing views; transitions animate additions and removals.
options.explanation: Property animations modify stable views, while transitions animate structural identity changes.

options.text: Property animations use UIKit layers, while transitions are handled by Metal.
options.explanation: Both concepts are core parts of the unified SwiftUI animation pipeline.

options.text: Property animations cannot use spring curves, while transitions require springs.
options.explanation: Both property animations and transitions can use spring curves and timing curves.

options.text: Property animations require withAnimation, while transitions never need withAnimation.
options.explanation: Transitions require an animated context like withAnimation to trigger.

options.explanation: .combined(with:) merges two transitions so both execute simultaneously.

options.text: By nesting the view inside an intermediate UIKit UIView container.
options.explanation: Transition combination is a native SwiftUI API and requires no UIKit container.

options.text: By passing an array of transition strings to the environment modifier.
options.explanation: Transitions are structured value types composed via .combined(with:).

questions.prompt: Explain the differences between implicit animations and explicit animations in SwiftUI, and when to use each.

rubric.criterion: Defines implicit animations using .animation(_:value:) and scoped to a specific view and property
Defines explicit animations using withAnimation to wrap state mutations affecting multiple views
Explains when to choose implicit versus explicit based on animation scope and coordination

questions.modelAnswer: Implicit animations attach directly to a view using `.animation(_:value:)`. They animate changes only on that view when the specified value changes. Explicit animations wrap state mutations in `withAnimation`. They animate all views across the hierarchy that depend on that state change. Use implicit animations for isolated view effects, and explicit animations when multiple components or transitions must coordinate together.

questions.prompt: Why does a .transition() modifier fail to animate if the state change is not wrapped in withAnimation?

rubric.criterion: Explains that .transition defines how a view enters or leaves the hierarchy but does not start animation itself
Explains that SwiftUI needs an animated transaction context to interpolate transition frames
Notes that without withAnimation, the view appears or disappears instantly without visual interpolation

questions.modelAnswer: The `.transition()` modifier only defines the appearance and disappearance style of a view when its structural identity enters or leaves the hierarchy. However, transitions do not generate animation timing on their own. SwiftUI requires an active animated transaction to interpolate frames over time. Without wrapping the state change in `withAnimation`, SwiftUI performs an un-animated transaction, causing the view to appear or vanish instantly.

questions.prompt: How do modern spring animations handle interruptions from user gestures compared to traditional linear curves?

rubric.criterion: Explains that spring animations are physics-based and naturally preserve velocity and momentum
Explains that user gesture interruptions redirect the spring smoothly without visual snapping
Contrasts with linear curves that stop abruptly or restart from zero velocity

questions.modelAnswer: Modern spring animations use physical spring models that track position and velocity continuously. When a user gesture interrupts an active spring animation, the spring incorporates the current velocity and redirects smoothly toward the new target. In contrast, linear or traditional timing curves lack velocity state, causing visual snapping or awkward pauses when interrupted by fast user interactions.

questions.prompt: How does modifier ordering influence the effect of the .animation(_:value:) modifier in a view chain?

rubric.criterion: Explains that .animation(_:value:) only affects modifiers placed before it in the chain
Explains that modifiers placed after .animation are not animated and update immediately
Provides an example such as animating offset while keeping color changes instantaneous

questions.modelAnswer: In SwiftUI, modifier ordering determines animation scope. The `.animation(_:value:)` modifier only animates modifiers that appear before it in the view chain. Any modifiers placed after `.animation` update immediately without interpolation. For example, placing `.offset()` before `.animation` and `.background()` after `.animation` will animate position changes smoothly while changing background colors instantly.

questions.prompt: Describe how matchedGeometryEffect works and what requirements must be met for it to function correctly.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains that matchedGeometryEffect interpolates size and position between two views across identity changes
Mentions that both views must share the same identifier string and Namespace token
Explains that only one view sharing that identifier should be active in the hierarchy at a given time

questions.modelAnswer: The `matchedGeometryEffect` modifier synchronizes and smoothly interpolates frame size and position between two separate views across an identity change. To work correctly, both views must share an identical identifier and belong to the same `@Namespace` token. Additionally, only one view with that identifier should be visible at a time. This allows SwiftUI to morph seamlessly between them.
